summary: Defines MIB objects, in SMIv2 format, for managing dial-up modems and similar dial-up devices with SNMP. It was written on the standards track but is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of gauges and switches for checking on the modems that connect computers over phone lines.

questions: how to manage modems with snmp
subtitle: Standard objects for monitoring dial-up modems over SNMP

tldr.problem: Network administrators needed a standardized way to monitor and manage dial-up modems remotely using SNMP, but no common set of objects existed for this purpose.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1696 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module in SMIv2 format that specifies objects representing modem identity, line state, DTE interface configuration, call control, error correction, data compression, modulation, and statistics.
tldr.outcome: The MIB provided a common interface for monitoring modems across vendors and products, though it became obsolete as dial-up modems themselves became less common in the late 1990s. It is now Historic.

today: RFC 1696 is Historic. Although it was a valid standards-track specification, the widespread decline of dial-up modems in the 2000s as broadband became prevalent made this MIB obsolete in practice. SNMP management of modems is no longer commonly deployed.

sections.title: Overview of the Modem MIB
sections.content:
RFC 1696 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for monitoring dial-up modems and similar devices using SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol). The MIB specifies a minimum set of managed objects needed to observe and control modem behavior across vendors and products.

The module was developed for use with SMIv2 (Structure of Management Information version 2), the standard for defining managed objects in the SNMP framework. It extends the core MIB-II by adding modem-specific objects that can be queried or configured by network management applications.

The scope is limited to dial-up modems (devices that establish connections over telephone lines) and does not cover other types of data communication equipment.
sections.plainLanguage: This defines the list of things you can check or adjust on a modem using SNMP, the system that lets network managers control devices from afar. Think of it like a meter panel on a modem.

sections.title: Object Groups and Tables
sections.content:
The MIB is organized into several logical groups of related objects. The ID group holds manufacturer and model information to identify the modem (for example, its OID and product details). The line interface group tracks the modem's connection state (on-hook, off-hook, connected, reset, busied-out) and the line capabilities (the protocols it can negotiate, such as V.32bis, V.34, or MNP compression).

The DTE interface group controls how the modem interacts with the computer it is attached to: what to do when DTR (Data Terminal Ready) changes, whether to use synchronous or asynchronous mode, and inactivity timeouts. The call control group defines parameters for dialing and answering: how many rings before auto-answer, call setup failure timeout, result code mode, and handling of escape sequences.

Additional groups track error control and data compression protocols in use, the signal convertor group records transmission rates and modulation schemes, and the statistics group collects counters for calls, failures, and data transferred.
sections.plainLanguage: The modem's properties are split into groups: who made it, whether it's connected, how it talks to the computer, dialing rules, what error-checking it's using, what compression it's using, how fast the line is, and how many calls it's had.

sections.title: The Modem ID Table and Augmentation
sections.content:
The MIB uses a central Modem ID Table that lists all modems managed by the system. Each modem has a unique index (modem number) and corresponding rows in the ID table. Other tables augment this base table, adding additional columns of information for each modem.

The line interface table, DTE interface table, call control table, error control table, compression table, signal convertor table, and statistics table all augment the ID table. This design ensures that each modem appears exactly once in the ID table, with all its related information accessible via a common index.

The line capabilities are stored in a separate table that can have multiple entries per modem: one for each protocol capability the modem supports. Each capability entry includes the protocol OID, whether it is requested to be enabled (disabled, optional, or preferred), and whether it is actually enabled (granted) by the modem.
sections.plainLanguage: There's a main table listing each modem, and other tables plug into it to add more details. For capabilities, one modem can have multiple entries—one for each thing it can do.

sections.title: Line Protocols and Capabilities
sections.content:
A major portion of the MIB defines the protocol capabilities a modem may support. The standard lists identifiers for numerous ITU-T modulation standards (V.21, V.22, V.32, V.34 and others), ITU error correction and compression standards (V.42, V.42bis), and proprietary protocols such as Microcom Networking Protocol (MNP) variants 1 through 10.

For each capability, an administrator can request a configuration (disabled, optional, or preferred) via the enableRequested object. The modem then reports what it actually granted in the enableGranted object. If multiple mutually exclusive protocols have the same preference level, the modem chooses among them using its own implementation-specific rules.

This design allows inventory of modem capabilities and remote configuration of which protocols to enable, without requiring row creation or deletion.
sections.plainLanguage: Modems can support many different ways of talking to each other (like V.32, V.34, etc.). An admin can say 'I prefer V.34', and the modem will try to use it. The modem reports back what it actually is using.

sections.title: Call Control and Statistics
sections.content:
The call control group allows configuration of modem answering and dialing behavior: how many rings trigger auto-answer, the timeout for call setup, whether to send result codes (and in numeric or verbose form), and the action to take on escape sequences.

Call state and statistics are read-only. The call duration object reports the length of the current or last call. The connection failure reason object reports why a call failed, with codes for common causes: no dial tone, busy signal, no answer, training failure, carrier loss, inactivity timeout, protocol incompatibility, power loss, and others.

The statistics group provides counters that accumulate over time: rings that went unanswered, incoming and outgoing connection completions and failures, dial attempt failures, retrains, and categorization of connections by speed (2400 bps or less, 2400-14400, greater than 14400). Additional counters track error-controlled and compressed connections, compression efficiency, and bytes and frames sent and received.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tell a modem how to answer calls and what to do with escape codes. The modem then keeps track of how many calls succeeded, how many failed and why, how many bytes it moved, and what speeds it achieved.

sections.title: Practical Use Cases
sections.content:
An administrator might use this MIB to build a management dashboard showing the state of all modems in a large dial-up access server. The modem ID group reveals which products are in use. The line state object indicates whether each modem is idle, connected, reset, or busied-out for maintenance.

Call control settings can be adjusted across multiple modems to enforce consistent policies: for example, setting the rings-before-answer to 2 on all modems, or configuring the inactivity timeout to 30 minutes. Capability tables allow verification that all modems support desired protocols and enable/disable them as needed.

Statistics tables help identify problem modems: one with a high failure rate suggests hardware issues, while high retrains indicate line quality problems. Speed breakdowns help track the proportion of calls at each speed tier for capacity planning.
sections.plainLanguage: A manager can look at all modems at once, see which ones are busy or broken, change settings on many at once, and see which modems are hanging up a lot or going slow.
